speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will I be allowed an opportunity to speak on that point of order?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
I will recognize the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) on the point of order raised by the hon. minister, but I do not think it is reasonable to suggest, with the state of the argument at this point, that the Chair can find a case of privilege in the remarks raised. I say this because it is important for the Chair to distinguish between debate which may not be acceptable to some members in some parts of the House at some times, and the actual matter of privilege. I think the hon. minister may or may not-and I make no judgment on it at all-have a point
of debate, but I do not see that I can find a question of privilege. Before a final ruling in that regard, I will listen to the hon. member for Saskatoon West.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think I understand the drift of what Your Honour will finally adjudicate on this matter. I fully subscribe to the point of view that there is absolutely no point of order. In case there is any doubt that my remarks were directed toward the hon. member for York South-Weston-and I think the blues will underline this-let me point out that I did not discriminate with respect to any member on the government benches. They all speak in high decibels because their position is very weak. I say that without regard to sex, origin or location. I did not in any way suggest that it was the hon. member for York South-Weston, for whom I have the greatest respect. All members of the House are equal regardless of their sex, which is a point the hon. minister does not understand. She does a disservice to her position when she suggests that such is not the case.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
I know the Minister of National Health and Welfare will be somewhat concerned when I direct my remarks to a male member of the House of Commons. Hopefully she will not rise every two minutes on points of order suggesting that I am attacking the males in the House.
I should like to talk about the minister concerned, because I think he is the basis of this entire motion. We as opposition members have the right to question and look at the actions of ministers of the Crown.
During the course of this debate we will be looking at the actions of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) who is responsible for reporting to the House on behalf of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women. Since the minister's appointment to his portfolio, he has reminded me of a character in A1 Capp's L'il Abner. This minister is the Joe Btfsplk of the current cabinet. Wherever he goes, whatever he does, there seems to be a storm cloud crashing around his head and lightning striking everything that comes within proximity of him. The minister has the propensity to get himself and the government into absolutely unnecessary difficulty. I make my remarks today as an opposition member because I want to be constructive and help the minister. He is one of the few elected ministers from western Canada so 1 have a very deep interest in his welfare. I know the minister fully appreciates that we have an interest in things indigenous to western Canada. Liberal cabinet ministers and dinosaurs are rare objects of antiquity which must be protected. In particular members from western Canada must attempt to advise and help the minister in the pursuit of his responsibilities. The minister has become a spokesman on virtually every western Canadian topic which has crossed a cabinet desk.
I was interested in an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press, a newspaper which has had a long tradition of supporting the Liberal Party of Canada. The editorial made reference to the minister's propensity for getting into difficulty. I bring this up
January 22, 1981

not for the purpose of embarrassing the minister-the Lord knows he does enough to embarrass himself-but I should like to read the conclusion of this particular editorial:
In many ways, Manitobans are fortunate that their sole representative in the federal cabinet is an active and ambitious man. There is reason for concern, however, that if Mr. Axworthy keeps puffing himself up at his present rate, one day he will simply burst.
This is the minister's home town paper, a paper of longstanding Liberal persuasion. I am concerned about the minister, so I am trying to explain the error of his ways and to put him on the right track. Hopefully, after this debate he will stand in his place and do the right thing. I will tell him what he should do. What we have today is a situation where the minister is attempting somehow to answer this very precise and specific accusation. I think it is fair to say that it is, in a sense, an accusation that he has manipulated the Advisory Council on the Status of Women contrary to the best interests of that body and of women in Canada today. As the minister responsible for that council he has taken an unprecedented step by this manipulation.
In his defence he does not deal with the particular topic. No, he has decided he will take another tack. He will rise in his place and recite for this House his many accomplishments in this government with respect to women's rights and women's issues in Canada.
When the question period started yesterday, or possibly the day before yesterday, the minister must have been thinking that maybe there would be a few questions asked of himself and the Prime Minister with respect to this issue. So, before question period, down the steps trundled the Minister of Employment and Immigration, the minister responsible to the Prime Minister for the Advisory Council on the Status of Women. He handed the Prime Minister an envelope which contained a list. The list, if we can believe, Mr. Speaker, was the list the Prime Minister tried to read into the record yesterday of all the great accomplishments of this minister. It was a self-serving document which was presented to the Prime Minister to defend the minister. The Prime Minister read it. Of course, it broke the place up. The place went into chaos. There was thigh-slapping and laughing and the Prime Minister was not able to finish reading it. I am sure if he wants to present us with copies we are prepared to have a look at it. But that is not what is at issue here.
I do not doubt the sincerity and the ambition of the minister. He wants to get ahead in Liberal circles. He wants to do a job which will lead to him being perceived as a Liberal leadership candidate. We want to ensure that he moves on and succeeds, since we think there is political advantage in it for us.
I want to say to the minister that the issue here is purely and simply: What has he done to the Advisory Council on the Status of Women? What has he done to the position of women across Canada through the action he has taken? I think these actions were taken foolishly and without serious consideration being given to the implications of women's interests in our
Status of Women
country. The speakers on the government side have stood in their places and complained because we are now in this debate. Somehow we in the opposition are to be held responsible for this whole mess. What an amazing proposition that is, Mr. Speaker.
I was not aware of the fact that the president of the advisory council was a paid-up member of the Liberal Party. I was not aware that she had been a candidate for the Liberal Party in the federal election. It certainly could not be said that the president was a person who was a political partisan in opposition to the government. This woman has said in public pronouncements that there was political interference with the operation of the advisory council. This is according to the record we now have, the minutes of the meeting of the advisory council.
They can flim-flam all they want about this issue. The advisory council was intended to be independent. The royal commission recommended that it report directly to Parliament, as opposed to a minister, but in its wisdom the government decided it should report to a minister. The underlying principle was that it would be independent.
The minister has broken the trust that he had with the women of Canada by interfering with a decision to hold a conference on the constitution of our country. The minister tries to answer the criticism by saying, "Well, of course, it really is a matter of timing, since now it would not serve any useful purpose for the advisory council to have a national conference on the constitution. Really, these issues are not on the plate of the government now. The issues have all been decided and the constitutional committee will now deal with these matters."
The fact of the matter is that while the advisory council made an admirable submission to the constitutional committee this conference would have been an opportunity for the council to have the benefit of a wide-ranging point of view from a number of women and women's organizations. And what is wrong with that? What is wrong with giving that kind of opportunity to the council, even though, as a result of the arbitrary time limit imposed by the government, it was obliged to make its submission before having had the chance to hear from the women of Canada?
The chronology will indicate that the planning went ahead as early as June of last year, with the minister's concurrence. The minister was to host a reception in September of 1980 when he would speak to the conference. Elaborate plans were made to hold this convention but it apparently had to be called off because of the translators' strike. Ostensibly, that is the reason why the meeting did not go ahead in September. That premise has been challenged by many women who were involved. They said there was an understanding with the translators that the conference would not be picketed. But be that as it may, it was decided to postpone the conference until February of this year. That was all done in the knowledge of the minister at the time.
Arrangements went ahead to hold the conference and Sheila Zimmerman was hired to organize it. Lucie Pepin undertook

January 22, 1981
Status of Women
to phone the Quebec speakers. The members of the advisory council were all set to hold this conference. The minister says he was then consulted about what his view was with respect to the conference. Mr. Speaker, I challenge the minister's version of the circumstances which took place. I now have information that prior to the time the minister says he was first apprised of these circumstances, namely, on January 5, 1981, a memorandum was sent to Doris Anderson from Hellie Wilson. It said, "Talked to Nancy Connolly-". Before I read the memo I must explain who Nancy Connolly is. She is the minister's assistant who speaks on his behalf. The memo reads:
Talked to Nancy Connolly yesterday. Minister wants regional conferences instead of national conference. Phoned Win.
I will deal with Win in a moment.
She thinks executive should discuss.
This memorandum indicates the minister's office initiated the discussion with respect to this matter prior to any discussion or any request for a discussion with the minister. If I am mistaken-and I do not believe I am-then the minister should bring forward facts to show I am wrong. He says he has an affidavit as to what happened at the meeting of the executive. He says there are these phantom documents which are somewhere in the possession of some unnamed lawyer. His defence relies on that premise.
Yesterday, in question period, I suggested to the minister that the honourable thing to do would be to stand in his place and suggest the whole matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. Then the affidavit could be produced. Evidence under oath could be given, as was done the last time that committee met. At that time we were able to get to the bottom of the issues, something which we will not be able to do here.
The fact of the matter is the minister has nothing but weak defences. He attempts to suggest that somehow these are affidavits which he is not prepared to disclose to this House. He is not prepared to table them. He is not prepared to give evidence under oath. There is only one conclusion that can be drawn when it comes to the question of who is telling the truth. That is that Doris Anderson's version is the correct one. The minister's version is incorrect.
This matter is causing serious concern to many women's organizations in Canada. The question of the credibility of the advisory council is of great concern to members on this side of the House. We want to see the minister produce the affidavit he talks about. We want him to bring it into the House.
Does the minister have the courage to table the affidavit in the House, or will this phantom affidavit be kept in his possession and in secret, undisclosed to anyone? When will the minister gain the courage to table this document in the House and to come before a committee of this House so that witnesses may be called and so that we may get to the bottom of what has exactly transpired. A very crucial issue is involved.
I have been informed that the secretary who took the minutes of this meeting of the executive which is the source of the dispute has been prohibited from speaking to anyone with respect to the taking of those minutes. She has been rendered incommunicado by the council members who remain. The council is disintegrating. Women's issues are suffering because of the serious damage done to the credibility of the council by the actions of this minister.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext: It is intimidation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
My colleague is quite right when she says that it is intimidation. The whole affair amounts to a scandalous interference into the affairs of an advisory council which represents women's interests in Canada. Why does the government not take the very reasonable suggestion put forward by our party, which is the basis of the recommendations of the royal commission chaired by Senator Florence Bird, who was appointed by the Prime Minister, try to restore some credibility to this group and have the council report directly to Parliament?
Why does the government not take the suggestions of the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) and have a wide consultation with women's groups across this country to ensure that it cannot be said that an appointment is political or that appointments are made on the basis of political persuasion. Of what is the government and the minister afraid? Why do we have this situation where the minister, the Joe Btfsplk of this cabinet, is responsible for women's affairs in the course of cabinet deliberations? Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the fact that you did not take out of my time the spurious and specious points of order raised by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
In conclusion, I would like to help the minister do a good job. Unfortunately, we face a majority Liberal government which has been known in the past for its arrogance and for moving ahead without sensitivity. If the minister persists with his present attitude, with attacking the president, as he did on the CBC program at six o'clock this evening, and with his single-minded determination to wheel control over this advisory council, then he has only seen the beginning of a fight. We in the opposition will stand for the interests of women in Canada and we will fight hard for their interests.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank you for flattering me when you called me Madam Maclnnis this afternoon. It would be very appropriate tonight if Grace Maclnnis, a champion of women and disadvantaged people, were here tonight. I know that she would speak eloquently on the subject and probably raise the quality of the debate somewhat. I would like to commend Doris Anderson, the past president of the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, and the staff and members of the council for their work. All of us should recognize that this group has made a considerable contribution, particularly in the areas of research and constitutional reform.
January 22, 1981

However, as many hon. members have already said, the reality is that the advisory council is a politically appointed council. It is primarily responsible to the government and the minister responsible for the status of women. Therefore, it is very difficult, no matter how well meaning its intentions, for the council to remain independent of the government. It is also difficult for this council to become anything more than a research, fact-finding group or to become involved in issues in a more active and militant way, which is what is needed if the situation for women is to change in Canada.
We know that most of the members of this group were appointed by the government through the minister and are Liberal Party members. This does not mean that they have not worked hard. The members of the council are largely a well-educated group of women who come from middle-class backgrounds. Undoubtedly they have worked hard and have produced valuable reports. In no way will I criticize the members of that council tonight.
However, I will criticize the structure and nature of this organization, which is quite impotent to act on behalf of the women of Canada and to press actively and militantly for much needed government reform. For example, there are certain groups which are noticeably absent from the council. The council is not representative of native women, although in fairness, it has spoken out on native issues. It is not representative of immigrant women who are doubly discriminated against in society today. The council is not representative of housewives, or women on low incomes, including single parents struggling on welfare. Representatives of the minority groups should be on a national advisory council and actively involved in trying to change their situation. My colleague indicated that women trade unionists are not actively represented on the council, with the exception of one Liberal appointee. Yet, a main goal of the council, and a major concern of the minister, is improvement in the situation of women in the work force.
Thousands of lonely, isolated older women, who represent the poorest group in our society, also are not represented on the council. This group has many concerns, and there is much need for assistance.
I shall not review the minister's interference in the affairs of the council because this allegation has been mentioned repeatedly and is well documented. The "haves" and the "have-nots" in society must join forces through a national women's organization, if women wish to bring about the changes which are needed. That is why our party has moved an amendment which would lead to the reorganization or restructuring of the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women.
We believe that such a council should be composed of delegates appointed or elected from women's organizations and trade unions in order to represent the interests of women across Canada. This newly-organized group should be accountable to women rather than to the government. It would work with the government as an agent for change.
Any effective national women's organization should have an advocacy function as well as a research function. There will be times when militant action will be justified. For example,
Status of Women
many of us were on the picket lines when the workers of Bell Canada struck last year. Most of those workers were grossly underpaid women. But where were the representatives of the advisory council? Perhaps they were there, but I rather doubt it.
I would mention the women in the steel industry in Hamilton. These women are pressing very hard to have jobs opened up to women. The minister has said that he favours women in non-traditional jobs, yet I do not believe that he or the advisory council was involved in supporting those women's movements. The advisory council has, as I have said, spoken out for Indian women's rights, and particularly in the case of Sandra Lovelace.
I am not aware that the council has taken militant action on behalf of immigrant women but I will come back to that in a minute.
It is important that the advisory council distribute information to women's groups across Canada and provide sound research, and this has been done. But there must also be a direct link with local women's groups. Action must be taken and documentation must be prepared regarding the problems which face women today. If Parliament believes that women's rights must be given higher priority, and I believe speeches made since I have been in the House indicate this is what all parties endorse, we must now act to make up for past discrimination.
If a new, more representative, council were to be formed, independent of government, I would certainly hope that Parliament and the government in power would continue to finance such a group. We must expect there will be criticism of the government if reform is the goal of a future women's organization. Doris Anderson and the advisory council have been critical in a constructive way until recently when, of course, they were deprived of this right.
I want to refer to some of the women's groups which I believe are outside the power circles in Canada. These need the help of an active and well-organized women's movement with a representative national council to speak on their behalf.
First, let us look at women in the labour force and trade unions. The Canadian advisory council last year published an excellent book called "Women and Unions". The progressive steps which have been made in recent years for more involvement of women in trade unions has been well documented. But research is not enough. If more women trade unionists were involved in an advisory council they would be pressing the government to encourage participation of women in the trade union movement and to recognize the efforts being made by bank workers, Bell workers, steel workers and the many other unions working primarily on behalf of women workers. It is not enough to say we want to see more non-traditional job opportunities for women. Women are starting at a different level than men. Their educational background is different. They must have decentralized apprenticeship programs to be able to get into non-traditional jobs.

January 22, 1981
Status of Women
A second and important group is homemakers, the women who work long hours, in the home, have few holidays, no benefits, and no pay. They are probably the hardest-working group in Canada. It does not matter from which economic group they come, "housewives" lack confidence and feel they are useless. If they are asked in a survey what they do, they say, "I don't work. I am just a housewife." This is a deplorable situation this kind of negative stereotyping which society imposes on women who work in the home. These people do a very important job of raising children and managing homes.
I hope we will bring in day care so that women who want to, can go out to work. We also need pension coverage and some form of pay for parents so that some may choose to remain at home and rear their children.
I would now like to refer the minister and hon. members of the House to an interesting task force on older women conducted by a women's rights committee. This was associated with the NDP in British Columbia and it travelled to the remote areas of the province. It involves local women in a non-partisan way. They were able to speak about their concerns and their desperate conditions. They organized ongoing women's groups in their own communities. This kind of task force should be a function of a national advisory council to reach out to older women from remote communities across Canada. Action must be taken to raise the incomes of older women who are the most poverty-stricken of any group in Canada. Decent housing, adequate pensions and accessible transportation systems must be provided for them.
I talked today with some of the representatives from the Indian Rights for Indian Women movement. They said they felt the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women has been great on research but short on action. The council did not make native women's issues a priority. It was too removed from local groups and issues. In fairness to the council, it cannot be all things to all people. But obviously this indicates there must be more involvement of women in local communities. Native women in particular must be represented if a national women's organization is to be effective.
Next I will speak about immigrant women. Many hon. members probably know, but if they do not know, they should, that immigrant women face double discrimination. They face discrimination as women and discrimination as immigrants. The Immigration Act discriminates against women and should be changed. Settlement services are very limited and unsuited to women's needs. I would be glad to go into this at some time with the minister. Immigrant women who are imported as domestics have no protection and should be able to become landed immigrants after they have put in a certain amount of time in Canada.
Finally I want to mention an important women's issue which has not been dealt with fairly in this House of Commons and which requires action from a national women's organization. We must work for repeal of section 251 of the Criminal Code to allow women who decide to have an abortion to do so legally and safely. I am not saying that we advocate abortion, but women must have a choice. Therefore, abortion must be taken
out of the Criminal Code. This is a highly-charged emotional issue. It has been debated twice in this House through private members' bills since I have been a member. However, I am very disappointed that members from other parties, particularly from the Liberal party, who brought in legislation supposedly in support of women, did not speak in favour of even retaining the present provisions for women to have therapeutic abortions. The members who spoke advocating a cutback and a restriction of the present policy, were all men. Reform of abortion law is an issue on which many Canadian women feel strongly. A movement for repeal should have a national voice through a democratically elected and representative national women's council. I could go on, Mr. Speaker, but I will leave it at that for now.
We in the NDP believe that there is an important role for a reformed Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women or a representative women's organization at the national level which perhaps should be given a new name. We believe it should not be a government appointed body. It should be a group which is truly representative of Canadian women in all walks of life. Therefore we have recommended in our amendment that the membership of a renewed council should be appointed or elected by and from organizations in this country, organizations which are actively involved in women's issues.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 take part in this debate with a feeling of sadness that something as important as 51 per cent of our population has been poorly represented by their elected officials in government, which is what prompted the presentation of this motion by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean).
I have listened to this debate today. I have heard different sections of society mentioned. I have heard about women in the labour force, and the underprivileged, who are denied their rights, as we all know. But I would like to address my remarks to a segment of our population that has not been defended to this point in time. I refer to the women in rural Canada, not just the farm wives but the farmers; women who run independent farms, women who farm with their husbands or their sons and, in some instances, with the assistance of their daughters. The National Council on Rural Development did a study on rural women. They discovered that the average farm wife works 29 hours a week in the field, in the barns, doing bookkeeping or carrying out some other function in a very productive part of our country, that of food production. We have a growing number of farm men who are holding full-time or part-time jobs off the farm. When they leave the farm, the balance of the burden of producing food falls to their wives or daughters.
There are still very many farm women who wish to be independent and be recognized as full partners in a farming operation. In 1978, the then spokesman for our party, the Hon. David MacDonald, brought to the attention of this House a
January 22, 1981

letter, which his colleague from Medicine Hat had received from one of his constituents, which I wish to read:
I work on the farm full-time (this often means 12 or more hours per day) during calving, seeding, summer fallowing and harvesting as well as doing all the bookkeeping and helping whenever necessary during other times. You will find that this is also the case with most of the women in this area, as it is no doubt in every farming community throughout Canada-
My husband has threatened to divorce me, and then hire me as a farm worker and so claim wages for me as an expense for income tax purposes. I am only joking, but I do think that the fact that this could be a solution, points out the foolishness of the present tax law. Just as silly is the fact that I could do the same work I do on our farm for a neighbour and get paid for it and my husband could hire a neighbour's wife to do the work I am doing here, pay her and deduct her wages as an expense.
It also hurts to know that women who work at their own job can file their own income tax. I have a teacher's certificate, but when I got married I decided to give up teaching to raise a family and help out on the farm. I feel this has been a good decision as far as the family is concerned and has meant a rewarding way of life to me-
The Hon. David MacDonald had this to say:
In the face of that reasonable proposition, could not the minister urge his colleague the Minister of Finance to include a provision of the kind suggested in a budgetary announcement? If this debate today does nothing else, I hope it will wake up the minister and the government who seem to be immobilized at the present time in the face of a pressing national issue.
I wish to speak on something which everyone in my part of the country knows and of which most rural communities are aware. Included in the Crosbie budget was a provision for spouses to be paid in unincorporated businesses. The majority of farms in Canada are unincorporated. That was not a new proposal. I have heard members of the government, including the minister responsible for the status, of women, say in this House that it would present a great tax relief if women, both farm women and women in small businesses, could be paid as full partners.
Even though this was brought in as part of our budget, we are still waiting for the legislation. We have not yet seen it. As we are approaching income tax time, I daily receive correspondence from my constituents asking what they should do. They point out that they have been paying their wives on the farm a salary since February 18 and so far, they do not know what is going to be done.
I wish to refer to something else that is very important in the farm community, the use of credit. As we know, credit is very important and not just to the man on the farm. It is very important to the woman who is a full partner, or one who is trying to enter the farming enterprise on her own.
The Farm Credit Corporation, a federal organization, despite all the statements made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) when he met with rural women in Ottawa to the effect that he would rectify this wrong, still discriminates against farm women. In fact, when most farm women apply to the Farm Credit Corporation, they do not even get to fill out the application form. The first question is, "What credit rating do you have?" With the present banking system, which is under federal jurisdiction, in most cases women are denied a credit rating of their own.
Women should be able to apply for a farm credit partnership loan. The policy of the Farm Credit Corporation entitles
Status of Women
individuals to apply for a loan up to a maximum of $200,000 and partnerships up to a maximum of $400,000. This federal organization, which is under the control of this government that is supposedly so proud of what it has done for the women of Canada, says that if a husband and wife are full partners, it will only lend up to $200,000, not $400,000 as would be the case if the two partners were men.
The Minister of Agriculture had some very encouraging words about how farm women in Canada can assist in taking their rightful place in this country. The minister, whom some of us recognize as tired, becomes very condescending. This is what he said to the rural women of Canada:
Farm women can help by opening up new lines of communication with urban consumers. Tell them that Canadian food products are of higher quality and nutritional value than almost anything we can import. Tell them why it is better to make cabbage salads in the winter than to waste their money on imported lettuce which is almost all water.
That is as condescending as what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said to the poor people of Canada, "reallocate your spending priorities". The farm women have much more to offer than merely telling the women of Canada to make cabbage salads rather than lettuce salads. The province of Ontario has credit guidelines which reflect equal credit opportunity. The federal government does not have guidelines to ensure that women are not discriminated against when they seek credit to continue in an operation, not just farming, but other enterprises as well.
We heard a representative of this government tell the farm women of Canada that if they want to make their presence felt, they must learn to lobby for the things they want. The reason this debate was brought forward is because the women of Canada were starting to lobby for what they wanted. At that time the minister said, "Don't lobby now because it may be inconvenient, it may embarrass our government and we are having another conference at that time." Is that any way of assisting the women of Canada to stand up and take their place alongside their male counterparts?
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, we on this side have stood and spoken for the rights of women. We have had spokesmen, spokeswomen, or spokespersons. We in this party do not have a problem. We can say spokesmen, spokeswomen or spokespersons. No member of my party has criticized me for saying that. There is no such problem on this side. I would, however, like to say that we have worked hard and diligently. We will continue to work hard as members of the opposition to ensure that women can take their rightful place among the workers of Canada. We find it very difficult to do this with the present minister. I heard a government member say that the minister is in a pillory. I doubt that very much because I do not think he could get his head through the hole.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not an expert on the Advisory Council on the Status of Women, but I think I understand something about fair play. I have known the minister for many years. Quite frankly, this motion

January 22, 1981
Status of Women
strikes me as something of a smear tactic to destroy his reputation and credibility. That is what prompts me to speak. What is the motion we have? The motion accuses the minister of and condemns him for his blatant interference as the minister responsible for the status of women, in the plans of the advisory council to hold a constitutional conference, and demands the resignation of the minister. It refers to "blatant interference". I have been reading the speeches given earlier today and I have listened to all the speeches tonight and 1 have not seen or heard any evidence of interference. We have heard a great litany about his alleged sins in the discharge of his responsibilities as minister. I am not surprised that the opposition is not impressed with his record. When have members of the opposition ever been impressed with the record of any minister on this side of the House on anything? If that were the criteria for resignation, then why stop at the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy)? Why not ask them all to resign?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext: Good idea.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
What makes members opposite happy about anything they do? It seems to me the only grounds on which they are demanding his resignation is that he blatantly interfered.
Let us have a look at what he did. What is this heinous crime he is alleged to have perpetrated? What was his statement here today? He said that the only time he became involved in their discussions was when they telephoned his office asking if he would meet with them to discuss the matter. He said that contrary to allegations that have been made, never at any time did he deal directly with members of the committee or of the council. He said they approached him and he met with them on a Friday morning. They asked him for his opinion and he gave it to them and he said that was the last contact on that discussion. Is anyone seriously suggesting that a minister of the Tory cabinet did not give his opinion on something when he was asked? I suggest not at all.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext: What is the point?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
The point being that I see no evidence here whatsoever that he blatantly interfered with anything, yet that is the only ground stated in the motion which calls upon him to resign.
The hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) says that somebody in his office called somebody or wrote a memo to somebody or somebody said this about that. That is a big deal, but is that interference? Let us get serious.
I would like to say something about Doris Anderson. I have known Doris Anderson for some years. I have a high regard for her and I like her. I supported her when she ran as a candidate in a byelection in 1978. She made a decision to resign. I regret that decision. I think it was a wrong decision and I think it was an unfortunate one. I have nothing else to say about it. She made a decision and that is it. 1 happen to
think the opposition has done her a disservice by fanning the flames of this incident into a great cause celebre which they have somehow painted as a blood feud between the minister and virtue.
What has really prompted this motion? I happen to think this is another chapter in a clear pattern by the official opposition in particular to destroy the credibility of this minister. When the hon. member for Saskatoon West suggested that this matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections I could hardly believe it. I am a member of that committee as is that hon. member. I sat through its hearings when we dealt with a previous matter relating to the minister.
Was the minister treated fairly by the opposition at that time? I suggest he was not. There were two issues and I think I have to make reference to them. There were two issues that came up. The first was, he was said to have made a decision concerning the entry into Canada by a person his department approved, which affected the fortunes of a small business in which he had a small interest. Very early in the evidence before the committee it was clear to anybody that the decision was made by officials in his department and he knew nothing about it. That was clear to anybody.
The second issue before the committee was an allegation that by virtue of the fact that the minister had a small interest in what you might call a family business, he was party to a contract entered into to provide employment for a handicapped person. It was quite clear very early in the evidence that he knew nothing about this decision and that he benefited in no way. Did that end the matter? No, that issue dragged on for weeks and weeks and weeks during which there were rumours, innuendos and fishing expeditions by the official opposition. It stretched the credulity of any impartial person to know that this was going on. If any group in that regard could be called impartial I would suggest it was the press, and members of the press who attended whom I spoke to said it was the biggest yawn in years and they simply stopped coming. It was a nothing story. There was simply nothing there; it was a hollow charge, a bum rap and nothing came out of it. That apparently is the route they want to go again. They want to go on another fishing expedition. They want to destroy the reputation and the credibility of the one minister this government has elected from the west.
I have known the minister well for 15 years. We worked together as ministerial assistants back in the 1960 s. He is an honest, decent and sincere man. Some of you are aware of the fact that I am chairman of the Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped. On several occasions during our hearings we met with the minister, and I can say quite sincerely that he spoke with some passion, fervour and most persuasively about his commitment on issues affecting women. That was the conclusion I believe members of all parties who served on our committee came to.
This brings me to the next point. This motion refers to changing the mandate of the advisory council enabling it to report directly to Parliament. This issue has somehow now
January 22, 1981

been elevated to a great question of principle. Our committee looked at that idea with an open mind. It seems there are two arguments you can make. I do not think they have anything to do with great questions of principle. You can say they should report directly to Parliament, and that is fine, or through a minister. A strong argument can be made for reporting through a minister because it may well function better in that at least you know there is one person in the cabinet who is on the hot seat, on the hook, is responsible, and people look to him to perform his duties. If he does not perform the duties he is assigned, he knows he will be on the hot seat in Parliament.
If the council reports to Parliament in general, no one person is really on the hot seat or on the hook in the same way. Therefore, I think a very strong case can be made that it is preferable to have a minister responsible.
What is wrong with responsible government? We all extol the virtues of that, but suddenly there is something wrong with having a minister responsible for his duties in Parliament. This principle does not bother me at all. I welcome it. In fact, I suggest this is one with which we all agree.
If we look at what is going on we will find five points that I would like to cover. They indicate what this debate is all about and how it strikes me.
First of all, there is no blatant interference. I would suggest there is no interference at all. A request was made for an opinion. The council received the opinion and it then made a decision. As to how much its members were influenced by that opinion, I do not know. They may have been influenced by it greatly or not at all. They asked for it and they received it. That is not interference.
The second point is that hon. members say they do not like his record. What record do they like on this side of the House?

speechtext:
It is pretty clear to me that this is another chapter in the attempt to smear this minister. The opposition is clearly trying to destroy the credibility of the present council, and it seems to me they feel that unless the council reflects their views somehow it has gone astray, the members are lost souls, sheep without a shepherd and should be restructured and brought into line.
The clearest point to me of this whole debate is that those who are guilty of blatant interference are those who want to interfere with the decision freely made by that council, and that is the opposition. They want to interfere. It is not members on this side of the House who want to interfere. They made a decision, it is their decision, and we respect that decision. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just been treated by the hon. member for Don Valley East (Mr. Smith) to almost as big a pile of that smelly stuff we
Status of Women
spread on the fields out west as we got from the minister earlier. The hon. member says he read the speeches and listened to the debate this evening but sees no evidence of interference. He obviously did not read the speeches very carefully. He did not listen to the debate very carefully, so 1 will put the evidence on the record again. Perhaps the hon. member will appreciate hearing the words I will read in a moment. I understand that he has some legal training. Perhaps he can appreciate facts, and perhaps he will make the logical and rational decision everyone else in the country is making, namely, that there was blatant and overt interference. I have in my hand a chronology of the events preceding the aborted constitutional conference. It starts earlier than January 5, but January 5 is where I will start this sad story of interference. In the interests of saving time I will pick it up on January 5 from a document I have in front of me which reads as follows:
Doris Anderson is away. Heliie Wilson speaks with the minister's office and reports that the minister wants regional conferences instead of a national conference. Heliie Wilson stops the press releases and letters from going out as scheduled. Two press releases-one to CTV and one to The Globe and Mail- have to be recalled by courier.
The following is a chronology of events for January 6:
Doris Anderson returns to the office and reads Heliie Wilson's memo about the minister's wishes. Doris Anderson phones Win Gardner-
I will talk about Win Gardner later.
-who agrees that the minister probably doesn't realize how damaging a postponement or cancellation would be to the Council. She says no former minister interfered with the Council this way.
Win Gardner is a Liberal appointee. She is a devoted and active Liberal and, as we will see in a few minutes from her own testimony, a close friend of the minister. She says, and I quote:
Doris Anderson phones Lucie Pepin but she is on holidays. Doris Anderson phones Nancy Connolly, the minister's assistant and explains that cancelling for a second time would be extremely damaging to the credibility of the Council. Nancy Connolly says the minister seems determined. Doris Anderson asks to meet with him.
Sheila Zimmerman-
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) knows Sheila Zimmerman.
-completes a progress report on the conference at Doris Anderson's request.
The following is the chronology of events of January 7:
Doris Anderson is home ill. She talks several times to Win Gardner and Nancy Connolly. Nancy reports that the minister is determined that the conference must be changed and regional conferences held instead. Win talks to Nancy and Heliie. Win asks that the whole executive meet with the minister. Doris and Heliie agree. The meeting is set for Friday, January 9, at 1 p.m. in the minister's office.
The following is the chronology of events for January 8:
Executive members get together for drinks and later have dinner at Nancy Connolly's. Doris Anderson learns for the first time that Lucie Pepin had not told Quebec participants that the February 13-14 date was firm.
Then we get into the meeting of January 9, of which the minutes are much more detailed. In fact, they were taken verbatim in shorthand, and I have a copy here. The minutes talk about the discussion. The hon. member for Don Valley East said there was no evidence of interference. According to the chronology of events I have here, Win Gardner said no

former minister had interfered that way. What does Win Gardner say on January 9 after she has talked to the minister? Win Gardner's statement is as follows:
My reasons for voting for cancelling the Conference on Women and the Constitution has nothing to do with the fact that the minister is a dear and close personal friend of mine. I am voting for cancelling the conference because we looked like fools the last time and 1 am not ready to look like one again and put our minister in an embarrassing situation toward his government.
That is a quote from Win Gardner. The hon. member says he was here, paid attention and is not aware of any interference. The hon. member obviously must have about three and a half inches of skull if he does not recognize that for what it is, proof of blatant interference.

speechtext: Opinion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
It is not opinion; it is fact. The minister says he has not seen this, but he knows it is not true because somewhere hidden away in the bowels of some lawyer's office is an affidavit. Well, where is this affidavit? Let us see this affidavit. Pleading for his old friend, the hon, member for Don Valley East related the tale of the minister's appearance before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections in relation to some questionable dealings in Winnipeg. Perhaps the hon. member remembers that at that point in time the minister volunteered. He was confident of his innocence of any suggestion of wrongdoing and anxious to prove that there was no evidence of wrongdoing.
He himself moved in this House that that matter be referred to committee so that he could prove his innocence. We challenge him to do that now. If the minister is confident that he did not interfere-I do not believe him, and nobody else in the country believes him-let us refer the matter right now to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, just as the minister did on the previous occasion to which the hon. member referred, and let us examine it. Let us bring this affidavit before the committee and find the truth. Let us examine the information and find the truth. If the hon. member is so confident about the minister's side of the story, what is there to fear? It could all be cleared up in a day. Why not have this cleared up?
The hon. member for Don Valley East says that all we have in mind is to destroy the reputation of the minister. The minister is walking from one cow plop to another. He is destroying himself with one inanity after another. It was not us who went through these machinations with regard to the National Advisory Council on the Status of Women which the minister supervises. No one on this side of the House tricked him into trying to postpone this conference in his devious way. He did it all by himself.
Was it Fotheringham who said, "The guy is going downhill faster than Steve Podborski"? He is disappearing. This man came here a few months ago with a tremendous reputation as a world-beater from the west who would revive the Liberal Party in western Canada. He was to be the hero and champion of women in Canada. He was to look after their interests. All we
see is a puff of snow down at the bottom of the hill as he disappears down the hill and into deserved oblivion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext: The minister stood here tonight, and even if one had not been to the same meeting Laura Sabia had been to in Toronto at which the minister talked in his pompous, patronizing manner, one could see from his manner here tonight that Laura Sabia perceived his character exactly. The minister is pompous and patronizing in his view and pompous and patronizing toward this House and toward everyone. I think it would not be parliamentary to put on the record some of the comments I heard in Calgary after his appearance there. Is this pompous minister going to save the Liberal Party in western Canada? The fact is that the minister was caught red-handed abusing his position and failing miserably in the tremendous responsibility he has as minister responsible for the status of women.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext: Is this the best you can do for an opposition day? It is unbelievable.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Proof of misuse, interference and abuse of his position is available. It is here in the minutes of the meeting of January 9, and hon. members know it, as do the women of this country.
The minutes of that meeting of the executive council of January 9 are really something. One after another these appointees, these loyal Grits, these loyal Liberals, have said, "The party comes first. Our responsibility to the advisory council and to the women of Canada comes second. We must not embarrass the government, we must not embarrass the minister, we must put them first and foremost, and only then will we look after our responsibilities to the women of this country who count on that." The minister knows darn well he was caught red-handed. So when he stood up in the House this afternoon, what did he do, besides demonstrating his patronizing pomposity? He made some erroneous comparisons between his performance since the election 11 months ago and the performance of our party during our short tenure in office. He said that the Progressive Conservative Party is all talk but no action. He said that while we were in office, no action was taken on behalf of the women of this country, but that in the short few months he has been in office, he has put in all kinds of programs to help the women of Canada, and that he has the proof for that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Let us look at the record of what happened during the PC tenure in office and during the equivalent time, the first nine months, when this Liberal government was in office with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) who is also in charge of the status of women. He has both jobs as well as being in charge of the status of women. When the Progressive Conservative government was in
January 22, 1981

office, we created 301,000 jobs-these are Statistics Canada figures-of which 218,000 jobs were for women, or 72.5 per cent of the jobs created were for women.
In comparison, this minister who says that he does not talk about these things, he just delivers, he just produced action on behalf of women as the minister responsible for employment and immigration and for the status of women, says that during his first nine months in office the government created 165,000 jobs, a little more than 50 per cent, of which 91,000 were for women, only 65 per cent of the jobs as compared to 72.5 per cent when we were in office. In other words, during his nine months in office he produced 42 per cent fewer jobs for women than did the previous government, and yet he had the gall this afternoon to speak about outperforming the Hon. Ron Atkey. If you do not believe it, ask him. We asked Statistics Canada and we find that, as a matter of fact, if he wants to catch up to the Hon. Ron Atkey, he needs to do two and a half times better.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
But when your case is weak, you rely on whatever you have. You grab and you make erroneous statements, in the hope that those in the opposition will not be able to catch up with you, will not have the facts and figures, so you can make these absurd statements.
He was followed, on behalf of the Liberal side, by his seatmate, the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola), who said-this shows her interest in the Advisory Council on the Status of Women and it shows her interest in the important work that that council could and should do-that she was not concerned with the fact that there had been two or three resignations, that she wanted ten resignations, she wanted the resignation of every single person who had the character to vote in support of Doris Anderson, to vote for the continuation of this conference which had been widely advertised, which had been postponed once and which was so important to the women of this country and to the groups which sponsored it. Ten women voted with Doris Anderson and the Minister of State for Mines said she wanted the resignation of them all. She thought it was absolutely intolerable to have even one single person on that council who does not put loyalty to the Liberals first. But there were actually ten people who said that their first responsibility is to the council and to the women of Canada. The minister said she wanted their resignations. That is because the government wants a really tame council; then they will be in good shape. They want a tame council who will know that what is good for the Liberal Party is good for the women of Canada. Yes, sir.
But there are a few women in Canada who do not agree with that. It might surprise members opposite to realize that. These women have been writing. Here are a few letters which they wrote. My colleague, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) mentioned that the letter, which just happens to be on the top of the list, is from the president of the Willowdale Association. Perhaps the hon. member for Don Valley East should have a talk with this individual who
Status of Women
clearly disagrees with virtually everything he had to say. Perhaps he could get her resignation also. Clearly this woman does not put the Liberal Party first. She thinks the Advisory Council on the Status of Women has important work to do and she supports Doris Anderson. I think you should demand her resignation because one rotten apple will spoil the barrel and you cannot tolerate these people who do not put the Liberal party first.

She is not the only one. Here is a telegram from Lynn MacDonald, president of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women. She writes:
-deeply concerned over possible cancellation of women's conference on the constitution. Representing over 150,000 national and regional women's organizations, we feel it essential to disseminate information prepared for the council and to receive opinion on all areas of concern to women who will be affected by constitutional change. Many of these have yet to be considered. We urge that the conference be held as planned in order that women benefit from the positive initiatives already taken by your council.
There are 150,000 organizations. That is terrible. Imagine that. They do not think that the minister responsible has the last word. How disloyal these people are not to accept that the Liberal Party knows best. For goodness' sake, you would think they would know. They should stay home and leave things in the hands of this brilliant minister because he has their interest at heart. Just believe him, talk to him, he will tell you. It is absurd.
That is not the only letter we have. There is a whole list. -wishes to commend your recent efforts to ensure the Canadian women's constitutional conference in February becomes a reality. The association feels this conference is necessary and supports the position you have taken.
This is addressed to Doris Anderson.

On behalf of the 30,000 members of the Federation of Women's Teachers' Association of Ontario I would like to congratulate you on your stand that the conference on women and the constitution should go forward. It is essential that these issues be discussed in a national public forum. That your executive fails to see the urgency of this matter is deplorable. We applaud your action and hope that your council will reverse the executive decision and show that it really is concerned to carry out its mandate.
They are saying that they are concerned to carry out their mandate and not just concerned for the political welfare of the minister and the party which appointed them. These are the people who write and say they are concerned about the fundamental issue. Surely sensible members over there will recognize that the work of this council is of vital importance. The royal commission of ten years ago established that beyond a doubt. Surely members recognize the wisdom of the recommendation contained therein, that the council must report to
