speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rather surprised tonight to see the speakers chosen by the opposition party because we always see the same faces, people who are called hit men, people who are needed when the opposition party has no idea what to say or what to do. They call in their strong-voiced frontbenchers who during the famous debate on the question of privilege involving the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) had an opportunity to make speeches in the House for a few days and then sit in committee for nearly two weeks to rehash the same thing.
It was very obvious to members in the House and members in the committee that once again they were wasting the time of the House and of the committee because they are simply frustrated for having spent so little time in office, one in particular who did not make it into the cabinet, who feels quite bitter and now seeks in every way to get rid of his bitterness so he can relax a little.
Even more astonishing, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that every day in the first two weeks of this session we heard people clamouring for an emergency debate on the North-South dialogue, the constitution or the economy. But what is the topic for today, the first allotted day? A topic which we on the government benches recognize as being very important but which has never been one of the priorities of the opposition, if their attitude in recent years and recent months is any indication.
It will be recalled that the Minister of Employment and Immigration responsible for the status of women made himself available to members of the opposition for almost 20 hours during the study of his department's estimates. Out of those 20 hours, Mr. Speaker, we spent perhaps 20 minutes discussing the status of women because hon. members opposite felt that the subject was not that important. And now, here they are brewing a storm in a teacup, making a mountain out of a molehill because of a resignation, because the members of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women could not see eye to eye on one subject.
Of course, this decision may seem surprising, Mr. Speaker, but I believe that it is normal and to be expected on the part of the opposition. I would like to come back to the decision of the Canadian advisory council on the Status of Women to postpone the February meeting, and to refer to an article published last week in Le Devoir, which said that the Federation des femmes du Quebec had indicated to the minister and the
members of the advisory council that the mid-February date was definitely unacceptable to Quebec women, and I quote:
Once again, the Conseil du statut de la femme in Quebec did not receive any official invitation to take part in the conference to be held on February 13 and 14. The president, Mrs. Claire Bonenfant, was to present a paper on women and the Constitution at the fall conference.
As it was decided in the last minute to reschedule this conference which had unfortunately been cancelled in early September, no one had been informed and the Advisory Council had regrettably not yet taken the necessary steps to notify everyone that this meeting would be held. The Quebec participants therefore could not attend the conference, Mr. Speaker, and I believe that a debate on the Constitution without the participation of some rather important members of this federation representing Quebec, namely, the Conseil du statut de la femme du Quebec, would not have been very successful. However, I believe that many participants had advised the Council-I have here a telegram from Mrs. Gabrielle Hotte, which was sent to the Federation des femmes du Quebec, and I quote:
-sorry but cannot attend the conference on women and the Constitution on February 13 and 14, due to our inability to prepare adequately at such short notice and the previous commitments of several participants.
This telegram was sent to the minister on January 19, Mr. Speaker, to advise him that if the conference was held as expected in February, some extremely important participants would unfortunately be unable to attend. There is still an aspect that I do not like to mention, but to which a reference was made in a Le Devoir article which I feel I must read, if you allow me, Mr. Speaker. It says, and I quote:
All this confusion about the conference points to a latent situation underlying the crisis in the council, namely the type of leadership given by Mrs. Anderson, a woman used to making her own decisions and who seems to find it very difficult to work with a team.
It is not the first time that the president has met with opposition from the executive and council members.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, when five of the six members of the executive voted against the president at the meeting, the hon. members opposite should have realized that the majority of council members supported those who wanted the conference postponed to achieve success and give the participants an opportunity to examine the amendments introduced by the government.
However, the president insisted she was the president, she was in charge, and she decided on her own to convene the conference against the wishes of most members of the executive. Later on, the invitation was withdrawn, and this week, the assembly of the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women decided by a majority of 17 to 10 to postpone the conference. Unfortunately, as was reported in the Le Devoir article, Mrs. Anderson is a woman who is used to making decisions single-handedly and who seems to find it difficult to co-operate with a team. However, Mr. Speaker, it is quite clear that an organization such as the advisory council must
January 22, 1981

work as a team and if the president was really unable to abide by the will of most members, she had to resign, even though members of the opposition and some women as well as ourselves deeply regret it; however, such was the will of most members and she did not respect the wishes of the majority.
Under the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I do not understand why hon. members opposite wanted to debate the issue for five hours. Because of the opposition's inability to grasp the core of the matter accusations were made against my minister and allegations of politicalization and partisanship were laid against the Council, but naturally they were totally unfounded. There were rumors, insinuations, but no one has yet put before the House facts that would justify or give weight to suspicions of undue interference on the part of any one in the whole matter.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, let me go on to other aspects of the subject, one of which was brought up earlier by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) with regard to job creation in 1980. Again, Mr. Speaker, allow me to quote figures that do not quite correspond with those of the hon. member for Calgary Centre who was bragging about the fact that his hon. government, in which he unfortunately was not a minister, had created- almost 300,000 jobs, nearly 200,000 of which were for women.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, thanks to their outstanding competence, they managed to do many things in nine months but as the first piece of legislation was passed at the end of November, 1979, 1 doubt very much that their performance was so spectacular in 1979 that it did in fact help create jobs. Naturally, they may have felt the positive effects of the previous Liberal government and 1979 may have been a good year in terms of job creation. But 1 for one will talk about
1980.

Employment for adult women was higher by approximately
170,000	jobs in 1980, an impressive increase of 6 per cent, reflecting the strength in the service-producing sector, a sector relatively insensitive to cyclical weaknesses. It was above the annual average growth rate of 5.2 per cent for 1975 to 1979. Adult women accounted for 59 per cent of the over-all increase of 286,000 jobs in 1980. I think those figures speak for themselves as far as what this government and this minister has done in the first nine months of his mandate.
Reflecting the rapid growth of employment among adult women, the declining trend in their unemployment rate, established in 1979, continued in 1980. Their unemployment rate dropped from 7.7 per cent in 1978 to 7 per cent in 1979 and to 6.5 per cent in 1980. I think these figures are proof of the improvements taking place under this minister. Not only did members opposite ask for the minister's resignation as minister responsible for the status of women but the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett) went so far as to
Status of Women
suggest he should resign all his portfolios. I think these figures illustrate the fact that the minister who is responsible for employment and for the status of women gave his department the tools to be able to act positively on the needs of women in the employment market.
1 will go a little further with respect to the performance of this government in the last ten months. Examples of this are the special measures in the employment development program, the employment tax credit, Outreach, non-traditional training under CM1TP, advertising campaigns, affirmative action in the public service and the affirmative action in the private sector. Other examples are the eligibility for unemployment insurance benefits for fisherpersons, spouses and teachers and reduction in minimum weekly hours required for unemployment insurance. 1 will go deeper into each one of these measures, Mr. Speaker, if you will permit.
The first example 1 cited was the special measures in employment development program. In particular, Canada community development projects and the Canada Community Services Contribution Program include in their contracts a section where a hiring plan must be submitted which will take into consideration the employment problems of women, natives and the handicapped. Any project proposal which does not contain a hiring plan is treated as an incomplete application and is returned to the sponsor. In addition, part of the monitoring process is an examination of the success of the project in meeting its hiring plan. The Canada Community Services Contribution Program will be of particular assistance to women. It aims to help organizations provide needed community services such as day-care, community health care, crisis and information services, and home care services.
Based on 341 projects approved to date, approximately 75 per cent of the total expected, it is anticipated that 20 per cent of all projects deal with primary and secondary services geared to women. The most frequently recommended and approved activities under CCSP to date are:
-Battered women, rape crisis, distress centres;
-Daycare centres and related activities;
-Transition/halfway houses for women;
-Integration services to immigrant women;
-Women's centres, drop-in information centres.
This summer we will be seeing a job-creation program which was announced today by the minister. We will also have positive action programs. Once again, women, the handicapped and natives will be helped by the government's programs. This is another example where the fact of having a minister responsible for the status of women and employment and immigration has positive effects.
Another measure is the employment tax credit program, which was extended by this government. In addition, under the present employment tax credit program there has been a steady increase in female participation. Under this government women constitute 38.9 per cent of the participants. This

January 22, 1981
Status of Women
represents a real increase of 4.6 per cent over the fiscal year 1979-80.
If I may continue, Mr. Speaker, the Outreach program is another measure. It has proven to be a useful program over the years in assisting women to integrate themselves into the labour market. In July, 1980, the minister directed that the highest priority be given to Outreach projects serving women exclusively.
I had the honour for the last nine months to work as the parliamentary secretary to the minister, the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry. I know the time and effort which have been spent in our department to deal with these issues. Members opposite may bicker about it and can understand their frustration with respect to it. They were in power for nine months and were unable to achieve anything. They did not have the courage to come into Parliament for the first seven and a half months they were in government. I know that the actions taken by this government through this minister and his joint portfolios have been positive actions with positive results.
I would like to continue with the next measure, which is the non-traditional training under CMITP. Of major concern to educators, women's organizations and unions is the concentration of women in a relatively small number of occupations and industries. In 1979, over 60 per cent of all women worked in clerical, sales and service jobs. Yet the areas of high demand for workers are ones in which few women are employed.
We had to act on this matter, which is why we entered into the development of a manpower industrial training program. It was oriented toward giving special services to women who were training in non-traditional occupations. We paid 75 per cent, to a maximum of $178, to employers who hired women in these non-traditional occupations. In addition, up to 100 per cent of the training costs and complementary course costs, such as assertiveness training, will be paid. Some 200 occupational groups were identified as non-traditional, based on a 10 per cent participation rate in the occupation nationally.
One other aspect about which we hear criticism from the opposition is the area of the advertising campaign. I think that no matter how much we on the government side, and members opposite as well, feel obligated toward this issue and give it a lot of importance, we still have, as the government, the responsibility to ensure that the general public better understands this issue and better comprehends the fact that we, as the government, must act on it.
An area in which the commission has frequently received complaints is in advertising. Women's organizations, among others, say that women do not know about the services and programs which the commission offers. In light of this, a $1.1 million advertising campaign was developed for television and print. The English television campaign started in December,
1980,	and the French campaign has just started. In addition, a brochure entitled "A Women's Guide to Federal Employment Services" is presently being produced and should be available in the Canada Employment Centres by the beginning of April,
1981.
Another program with which the minister dealt, not as minister responsible, but as part of the cabinet, is the affirmative action in the public service program. This government feels strongly that the public service must set an example for the private sector by cleaning its own system of any systemic discrimination. Therefore, an affirmative action program has been launched in the public service. This program will include an assessment of the types of discrimination in hiring and promotion which keep women and other groups from participating fully in the labour market.
I could go on, Mr. Speaker, with respect to affirmative action in the private sector. Here we tried to arrange contracts with the private sector to encourage this type of affirmative action. I talked briefly before about unemployment insurance. I mentioned the reduction in the minimum weekly hours required. The Advisory Council on the Status of Women made recommendations about this to the previous Conservative government. They recommended it be changed, but that was rejected. This afternoon the minister quoted in the House a response given by Mr. Atkey, the minister in that government. The Conservative government rejected it because they did not think it was a priority. The reduction in minimum weekly hours required for unemployment insurance allows for 15 hours of work per week or one fifth of the maximum insurable earnings. The existing requirement of 20 hours of work per week had a negative effect in particular categories of workers, especially women. The significance of this change for women is illustrated by the fact that about one in every four women is a part-time worker, whereas only one in 17 men work part time.
These are just a few of the examples, Mr. Speaker. I would like to deal with the constitutional aspect in the minute of time which remains to me. I am sure that everybody recognizes- [Translation]
-that the contributions of the advisory council with respect to amendments to the charter to the Constitution have been positive and I would like to quote a statement made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) before the committee:
I must admit that the accomplishments of this council have greatly influenced the government.
Such advice from the advisory council has made it possible for the government to amend section 15 on the right to equality. To ensure that the principle of equality be observed in the very implementation of the act, section 15 was amended as follows, and I quote:
The law makes no exceptions and applies equally to everyone, and everyone has the right to equal protection and benefit of the law without discrimination because of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, age or sex.
This is a very important addition, Mr. Speaker, one which is appreciated by all the women of this country.

Mr. Speaker, on November 7 I directed a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who had stepped out of the House, and in his absence, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Irwin) gave the reply. My question concerned the amendments to the Criminal Code which would permit euthanasia along the lines of the 1969 amendments which permitted therapeutic abortion. The parliamentary secretary in his reply said that the issue of euthanasia was not a major priority but that the government would take cognizance of the issue and deal with it in due course.
Euthanasia is a sensitive issue. When I endeavoured to ask a supplementary question I was cut off by Madam Speaker. 1 am sure that you are aware, Mr. Speaker, that the supplementary question is really the heart of any question posed in this House. My supplementary would have been phrased in the following words: Because of the tragic toll of 450,000 aborted babies since the Criminal Code was amended in 1969, will the government take action to amend the Criminal Code and to end this violation of the most fundamental of all human rights, the right to life.
The two actions, abortion and euthanasia, are closely related. They both bring about death on the pretext of improving the quality of life. 1 am sure that hon. members will agree that this is a horrible paradox. When the Criminal Code was amended in 1969, the point was made by the government that it was designed to permit abortions only when the physical and mental health of the mother was in peril. The added argument was made that it would end criminal abortions by human butchers in rooms in back alleys.
Every concerned citizen, I am sure, will agree that the killing of half a million unborn babies goes far beyond the need of therapeutic abortion. In fact, it amounts to the wholesale slaughter of the innocent. The tragic situation is an inevitable byproduct of a permissive age which ignores the Judeo-Christian ethic of the right to life and leads down the slippery slope of moral relativism. It is the medical profession which has had to bear the brunt of this tragedy. All members of the medical profession must take the Hippocratic oath and must swear that they will observe the declaration of Geneva which was adopted by the general assembly of the World Medical Association at Geneva in September, 1948. One of the major points in the declaration states as follows:
Adjournment Debate
I will maintain the utmost respect for human life, from the time of conception, even under threat. I will not use my medical knowledge contrary to the laws of humanity.
There are many quotations by doctors who, more and more, are reacting against the tragic position in which they are placed by the legislation. Here is one such quote:
Some time ago-after a tenure of a year and a half-I resigned as director of the Centre for Reproductive and Sexual Health.
That title is really a euphemistic description of an abortion clinic. The doctor went on to say:
The centre had performed 60,000 abortions with no maternal deaths-an outstanding record of which we are proud. However, I am deeply troubled by my own increasing certainty that I have in fact presided over 60,000 deaths.
Inevitably this has a brutalizing and dehumanizing influence on human beings which is reflected in the growing problem of child abuse and in marital and family breakdown. 1 believe, and there is evidence to confirm this, that in Canada the pendulum is swinging back again. There is a growing number of concerned citizens. They are represented by many members of the House who are strongly against the abortion bill arising from the Criminal Code amendments in 1969. They come from all sides of the House and their concerns are being made known through private members bills, questions and speeches.
At a time when the government is calling for a charter of human rights enshrined in the Constitution with the right to life as the number one priority, to continue to condone the slaughter of 65,000 babies a year is the height of hypocrisy and moral schizophrenia of the most dangerous kind. I would urge the government that rather than contemplating further amendments to expand the use of euthanasia-which I presume would be in the direction of the aged and the infirm- and rather than doing this in the name of improving the quality of life, because it is justified under the pretence of social purposes and social improvement, to instead introduce amendments to the Criminal Code changes that were made in 1969, which have done untold damage to the integrity of our basic institution of family life in Canada.
I would urge, Mr. Speaker, that this action be taken at the earliest possible moment.

The hon. member has raised an issue of considerable moral and legal complexity. As a study paper written from the ethical perspective for the Law Reform Commission of Canada as part of its Protection of Life project points out, the term euthanasia is used to mean so many very different things that its use confuses and begs more questions than it clarifies and answers.
The author of that study paper entitled "Sanctity of Life or Quality of Life" points out that some writers continue to use the term to mean what the Greek word literally meant, "a good death", and intends by that what others would now more

Adjournment Debate
generally label "allowing to die with care", a form of care which excludes killing. The more common and probably fixed meaning in our times is that of directly killing the dying patient. The author goes on to note that the use of the same words in these two different senses only covers up and blurs the essential distinctions between the two approaches. He cites a study published in the United States in 1976 which reads in part as follows:
Justifies a moratorium on its use . . . Formulation of any public policy dealing with these issues will consciously or unconsciously have to make these distinctions-
In response to the hon. member's question of November 7, no work is being done by the government on the subject of euthanasia. However, the hon. member may be aware that the Law Reform Commission of Canada in its seventh annual report of 1977-1978 listed euthanasia as one area in which working papers were being prepared. The description reads, and I quote:
This paper is an evaluation of how well relevant Canadian law (particularly the homicide laws) and legal theory actually protect and affirm the various rights and values raised by the issue of euthanasia in the medical context... If the commission concludes in this paper that present law is inadequate with respect to euthanasia, specific laws or models will be formulated by way of reform proposals.
However, I must add that the latest report of the commission, which was tabled in this House, indicates that the more particular concern of the working paper which is still to be published is the question of cessation of treatment.

GARRISON DIVERSION-REQUEST PRIME MINISTER DISCUSS PROJECT WITH PRESIDENT OF UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I rise this evening to expand on my questioning of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) yesterday.
There exists at this moment both a very real danger to Canada that the Garrison diversion project in North Dakota may go ahead full steam, and a real opportunity to make contact with a new administration in Washington, anxious to establish early and good working relations between our two countries. Members on both sides of this House have been encouraged by the interest shown by the new administration in Canadian matters. The fact that the President phoned the Prime Minister yesterday, his first day on the job, is an indication of the priority put on Canadian matters in Washington. Our very real problem is that the new Congress is not
January 22, 1981
informed on the situation with respect to the Garrison diversion project.
It seems to me there is a very real possibility that some of these new congressmen may be asked to make decisions on Garrison from a less than well-informed position. The governor of North Dakota is claiming to have heard "nothing official" from Ottawa. In his reply to me in the House yesterday, the Secretary of State for External Affairs pointed out that the Canadian government has indeed made numerous official representations to the U.S. government in reference to Garrison.
The newly-elected governor of North Dakota, Mr. Olson, has been making some very disturbing statements in reference to the Garrison diversion project and the effects the project could have on Canadian waters. Governor Olson was formerly attorney general of the state of North Dakota and, in his capacity as attorney general, he filed several lawsuits to force completion of Garrison in spite of Canadian objections. In a press conference held in Jamestown, North Dakota, January 15, Governor Olson threatened to bring an injunction against the Interior Department forcing it to free up the $5 million currently being withheld by the department pending clarification of the situation respecting Canadian waters.
Governor Olson told a joint U.S. lobby group against Garrison that work on Garrison should continue until the threat to Manitoba fishing and agriculture is proven. The very real danger of biota transfer and the resulting disastrous effects in Manitoba have been proven time and time again. Governor Olson has promised to resolve the dispute over Garrison in the first 18 months of his administration. His statements so far have led me to believe he is willing to keep this promise at the expense of the environmental integrity of Canadian waters.
Congressman Mark Andrews of North Dakota is a notorious supporter of Garrison. At a Canada-U.S. interparliamentary group meeting held in Calgary in August, 1979, which I attended, Andrews said that the only objectors to the Garrison project were "environmental zealots". This term would hardly apply to the government of Manitoba, members of this House, the Audubon Society on both sides of the border and top-rated American and Canadian scientists.
In a naive reaction to the freezing of the $5 million by the Interior Department, our Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) said that Canada now held a "veto" on the project. That was quoted in the Winnipeg Free Press of November 20, 1980. It is now clear that we not only have no veto, we have no voice in Washington.
It is absolutely essential that we form a parliamentary delegation to go to Washington immediately to explain our position to the newly-elected U.S. Congress. I wish to restate the need for this delegation so eloquently put by my colleague, the hon. member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) on January 13. Governor Olson seems intent on a confrontation with us and we have to get our case before the Congress now.
January 22, 1981

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: GARRISON DIVERSION-REQUEST PRIME MINISTER DISCUSS PROJECT WITH PRESIDENT OF UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government fully intends to pursue the Garrison diversion issue with the new U.S. administration, and will ensure it is raised with President Reagan at the earliest opportunity.
In the past, the government has actively made known to the U.S. administration and Congress the serious nature of Canadian concerns about the Garrison diversion project. We believe this effort has had some positive effect. While it is disappointing that the Congress allocated new funds for the project last summer, it is encouraging that the Department of the Interior subsequently deferred spending of funds associated with parts of the project which might affect Canada until consultations with Canada had been completed. We will be actively pursuing those consultations as a means of obtaining modifications to the project which would protect Canada.
The United States has given some important assurances to Canada over the years under a number of administrations. We fully expect the new U.S. administration to abide by its previous commitments, and its obligations to Canada under the Boundary Waters Treaty.
The government will be taking steps to make clear to the new administration and Congress and the new governor of North Dakota the serious objections which Canada has to any plan which would permit the entry of foreign biota into Canada through the inter-basin transfer of water. Thank you.

MUNICIPAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION OF CUTBACK OF COMMUNITY SERVICES CONTRIBUTION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise following a question which 1 asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on January 12 of this year. I asked him to reconsider his fiscal policies and the cutback in the Community Services Contribution Program by his government.
In response to my question the minister refused to reconsider either his fiscal policy or his expenditure plans in his budget of last October, yet we all know that his budget is not working. We have high interest rates continuing to plague the economy of the nation, unemployment is rising, the cost of living continues to increase and the number of bankruptcies are up. The budgetary justification for cuts from the Community Services Contribution Program is just not valid. The minister should, therefore, be reconsidering his economic strategy and the cutback in that program.
I suggested to the minister that he consider a new program of investment in communities across this country, replacing the Community Services Contribution Program in order to provide stimulus to the economy and to provide the much-needed services which the Community Services Contribution Program represents. He refused to consider that and simply referred back to his budget and his former expenditure plan. In spite of the economic facts, and we all know, and it is clear to us, that we have an economic slump and continuing difficulties with
Adjournment Debate
the cost of living and people being out of work, this government and the Minister of Finance just do not seem to be willing to take a second look, even in view of the harsh realities we are all presently facing.
If the minister and his government are so set upon sticking with their fiscal policies and expenditure plans, they should offer some substitute for the Community Services Contribution Program. If they are solely concerned with not spending more and with the threat of a rising deficit, do they not understand that spending can be an investment and can lead to further economic activity, thus creating wealth and in that way holding the deficit down? Why has the minister not substituted a program of low interest rate loans for municipal programs? If these cannot be direct loans by the federal government, why can they not at least be guaranteed loans which in no way would increase the expenditure of the government? This would involve money from the private sector and from the banks, which could be used to promote local municipal projects.
However, the minister and the government clearly have not been searching for any alternatives to the Community Services Contribution Program. They have simply shown a lack of care and concern about this very fundamental and crucial issue to all the communities of our country.
If the government had some real concern, I am sure it would come up with a substitute program and be willing to say so this evening. One of the clear strategies in the minister's budget, to which he referred when I questioned him in this House, is cutting back on federal expenditures, particularly in areas of provincial jurisdiction. This is simply a shell game, shifting the burden of the federal deficit from the federal government to provincial and local authorities and taxpayers. This game is causing real concern across the country, particularly at the provincial level. Provincial officials are concerned that this is just the first step in cutting back federal contributions to programs for people. For example, established programs financing legislation will soon be renegotiated with the various provincial governments. That program finances medicare, post-secondary education and hospitals and involves very large sums of money.
Provincial governments are concerned that the federal government will take the same attitude in those negotiations as it has taken with respect to the Community Services Contribution Program, which is simply to drop the program without any consideration of need or local authorities. The same attitude has been demonstrated by the federal government in its handling of policing costs under RCMP agreements. This government wishes simply to shift the burden from it to local governments. This does not in any way serve the people of the communities of our country.
The government may doubt that this program is needed or it may attempt to throw doubt on the need for this program, but let me tell the government and its members that I have been receiving letters from right across the country outlining the

January 22, 1981
Adjournment Debate
need for this program. There should be no doubt about the need for it.
I have one letter here, for example, from the town of Ladysmith, British Columbia. The council there passed a resolution calling for the reinstatement of the community services contribution program. The council says in this letter, and I quote:
The termination of this program will have a serious effect on the finances on the town of Ladysmith. The council is presently faced with a program of improvements to the town sewer system, which is estimated to cost $6.2 million .. . Unless further development within the town is stopped, it is essential that this program be proceeded with.
This refers to the sewer system program. Clearly, without the Community Services Contribution Program, development in the town of Ladysmith will stop. The council went on to say:
Without the expected contribution from the Community Services Contribution Program, the rates charged to the residents of the Town will be substantially higher than they otherwise would have been.
This is only one example of what is happening all across this country. This program is needed, and there is no way the government can say it is not needed and that through cutbacks in this area it is not hurting people right across the country. 1 have many other letters here, which are only a sampling. My time is up. I rest my case.

speakeroldname: Mr. Raymond Savard (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: MUNICIPAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION OF CUTBACK OF COMMUNITY SERVICES CONTRIBUTION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to reply to the question the hon. member put to the Minister of Finance in this Elouse on January 12.
As my colleague mentioned, the government decided not to renew the program because of its desire to maintain expenditures in line with revenues. I can assure the hon. member that this decision was not easily arrived at and that this was done only after careful consideration. First, there was the question of whether it was appropriate for the federal government to continue to subsidize services which, as far as jurisdiction is concerned, were in fact the responsibility of the provinces and the municipalities. The question was not whether this was a good program but rather who was going to pay for it. Second,
there was the question of accountability, of whether the government's responsibility was at issue; that is, whether the government responsible for collecting funds through taxation should not be the one responsible for the expenditure of its revenues. Third, the effectiveness of the program was considered from the point of view of future job creation and compared to other programs, which seemed to show a better return for the money. Finally, Mr. Speaker, as I have just said, tax cuts were also a factor which influenced the decision. In an effort to achieve greater government efficiency, we studied the advisability of extending the current program with a view to allotting funds to new programs or more pressing priorities. A decision not to renew community service programs would allow more funds to be assigned to more important programs in 1982-83. The challenge lies in determining where the housing priorities of the federal government lie for the 1980s. We shall continue to hold informal discussions with our provincial colleagues and other interested parties. The minister would like to see those consultations help in ensuring continued federal housing assistance, and those programs and priorities lead to a better distribution of funds among them.
Mr. Speaker, under this program, the federal government earmarked $400 million for municipal projects, of which $150 million were assigned to 1979 programs, and $250 million to 1980 programs. Over 3,000 projects in 1,000 communities have already received federal assistance. As the hon. member can see, that is a rather significant amount to provide local services to Canadians in each and every province. The hon. member referred specifically to the number of lost jobs. May I assure him that the number of jobs will remain the same under this program because federal assistance is guaranteed until March 1982.
